title: Entropy spectroscopy of a tunable two-site Hubbard molecule
authors: Uhjin Kim, Seokyeong Lee, Gibum Yun, Dongsung T. Park, Soobeom Choi, Sangwoo Jeong, Donghoon Kim, V. Umansky, Yunchul Chung, Hyoungsoon Choi, H. -S. Sim, Hyung Kook Choi
abstract: Determining which microscopic states remain thermally active when tunneling and interactions compete is a central question in Hubbard physics. Here we develop an entropy measurement protocol for a double quantum dot, extending the charge-based approach established for a single dot, and measure the total entropy of a tunable two-site Hubbard molecule realized in a GaAs double dot. By shifting both dot levels together at fixed detuning, the entropy is correctly probed with only a single charge sensor. As interdot tunneling increases, the system evolves from two atomic-like dots through hybridized molecular states to a merged single dot. Across this evolution, the entropy decreases as tunnel-induced energy splitting exceeds the thermal energy and suppresses the occupation of higher-energy states. The measurements resolve the diminishing contribution of antibonding states and the changing thermal contributions of hybridized singlet and triplet states, in quantitative agreement with a two-site Hubbard model. By distinguishing states with the same charge configuration but different orbital and spin content, entropy reveals how tunneling and interactions determine the thermally active states of the minimal Hubbard system.
summary: This paper reports on an entropy spectroscopy technique applied to a double quantum dot acting as a tunable Hubbard molecule. By measuring the total entropy, the researchers quantitatively track how the thermal population of quantum states changes as interdot tunneling increases. This method successfully distinguishes the contributions of different molecular eigenstates, providing deep insight into the interplay between quantum coherence and thermal fluctuations.
main_problem: The central question is determining which microscopic states remain thermally active when tunneling and interactions compete in Hubbard physics.
main_result: Entropy spectroscopy reveals that as interdot tunneling increases, the total entropy decreases because the energy splitting suppresses the occupation of higher-energy states.
method: The authors developed an entropy measurement protocol for a double quantum dot, utilizing a specific trajectory ($\delta$-axis) to circumvent measurement limitations with a single charge sensor.
model_or_system: The system is a tunable two-site Hubbard molecule realized in a GaAs double quantum dot (DQD). The physics is governed by the competition between interdot tunneling ($t$) and interactions, analyzed via the total entropy ($S$).
key_observables: Total entropy ($S$), Charge Sensor (CS) conductance ($G$), and the number of thermally accessible states ($\Omega$).
important_parameters: Interdot tunnel coupling ($t$), thermal energy ($k_B T$), and the detuning ($\delta$).
main_assumptions: The protocol assumes the system remains in thermal equilibrium with the reservoirs, and the $\delta$-axis trajectory is used to ensure the Maxwell relation depends only on the total DQD occupation.
figures_summary: Figures show the tunability of tunnel coupling, the evolution of entropy across different tunneling regimes, and comparisons between entropy extracted via the proposed $\delta$-axis protocol versus other measurement paths.
paper_structure: The paper first introduces the challenge of measuring DQD entropy, develops the $\delta$-axis measurement protocol based on Maxwell relations, and then presents experimental results showing entropy evolution as a function of interdot tunneling strength, confirming theoretical predictions for state occupation.
why_interesting: This work provides a direct, measurable thermodynamic probe (entropy) to characterize the competition between quantum tunneling and interactions in a minimal many-body system, offering insights into the nature of quantum phase transitions.
